paras: The manhunt and shooting of Wesley Fisher took place near Cumberland, Maryland, in late October and early November 1882, when Fisher, a young Black man accused of raping a farmer's wife, was hunted by armed citizens and shot by two private captors on November 3. He survived his wounds and was jailed amid threats of lynching, which the sheriff was reported determined to resist. Fisher denied the charge, was identified by the woman at a hearing, and was held for the grand jury.

According to her own account to a Baltimore American correspondent, Mrs. Frances Wolf, wife of farmer George A. Wolf, was attacked on a woods path about half a mile from her home on Sunday evening, October 29, as she returned from church in Cumberland. Her husband suspected Wesley Fisher, a youth of about eighteen who worked with his father as a blacksmith, and swore out a warrant.

Armed men from the neighborhood began scouring the woods, and the Evening Critic reported that citizens were "after Fisher with shotguns and a rope." Sheriff Shuck and a posse also searched, and the County Commissioners offered a $100 reward for Fisher's arrest. A Baltimore German paper reported mounting anger in Cumberland, criticism of the sheriff for letting the suspect slip away, and scorn for the small reward.

Between 8 and 9 o'clock on the morning of November 3, two young men, C. H. Slaughter and Andrew Johnson, found Fisher in Sanders' meadow at the foot of McNamee's Hill, about two miles north of Cumberland. A Cumberland dispatch said they had tracked him from a haystack by a patched shoe print and fired a shotgun and a pistol when he ran. The Baltimore American correspondent counted flesh wounds in the shoulder, elbow, hip and foot, while other reports gave three shots or wounds to the elbow, head and foot. With Joseph Brant, who had joined the chase, they tied Fisher and drove him in Brant's wagon through the city to the jail before most people knew of the capture.

When news of the capture spread there were "some threats of lynching," but the Somerset Herald's correspondent wrote that the jail was strong and the sheriff did not propose to give up the prisoner. Interviewed in jail, Fisher said he had spent Sunday gathering chestnuts and playing with boys, and that he fled after being warned that Wolf was going to shoot him, believing he would be killed if he gave himself up.

At a hearing before Magistrate Gonder on November 9, Mrs. Wolf identified Fisher, and a Black youth named Burke testified that Fisher had said he would have killed her if he had had the means. Fisher was committed to jail for the January term grand jury, and no report of an indictment or trial appears in the coverage found. On December 7 the County Commissioners divided the $100 reward equally among Johnson, Brant and Slaughter, a settlement the Frostburg Mining Journal called the best for "a small but somewhat vexatious matter."

Only white papers covered the case, from Washington, Baltimore, Wheeling, Wilmington, Memphis, Somerset and Frostburg, chiefly through wire items and Baltimore American specials. Headlines such as "A Candidate for Hemp" in the National Republican and "A Negro Ravisher Shot" in the Wilmington Daily Gazette treated the accusation as proven and a lynching as expected. The Baltimore American's correspondent wrote that Fisher had earned "swift retribution," and a Baltimore wire in the Memphis Daily Appeal predicted he would "meet with quick justice" if caught.

The Baltimore German daily Der Deutsche Correspondent used still harsher language, calling Fisher a "black devil" and hoping he would not escape the citizens' thirst for revenge. After the capture, coverage turned to the sheriff's resolve and printed Fisher's denial and alibi at length, though the Somerset Herald added that there was "no doubt" he was guilty.

Accounts of the alleged assault differ: the Alexandria Gazette placed it on Monday afternoon and a Baltimore wire on "last evening," against the Sunday date given by Mrs. Wolf and the reward notice. Mrs. Wolf told the Baltimore American she had seen her attacker several times, while Der Deutsche Correspondent said he had been wholly unknown to her.

reader.title: Manhunt and shooting of Wesley Fisher
bases: A Black man accused of rape was hunted by armed citizens reported to carry 'a rope' and by a sheriff's posse, shot and wounded by two private captors, and threatened with lynching once jailed, but no one was killed (A3, A11, A16).

Fisher survived: he was shot in pursuit by two private men and delivered to the sheriff, and the lynching threats in Cumberland were not carried out (A11, A16, A17). The episode is a threatened lynching, not a completed one.

The Baltimore American special (A11), a separate Cumberland dispatch (A16), the German-language Baltimore paper (A15) and the reward division (A19) independently agree on the capture, shooting and jailing.

accounts.label: Baltimore American correspondent
accounts.gist: Slaughter and Johnson ran Fisher down from his hiding place with pistol and shotgun, wounding him in shoulder, elbow, hip and foot, tied him and drove him to jail before the public knew.

accounts.label: Cumberland dispatch (Somerset Herald)
accounts.gist: The two tracked him by a patched shoe print from a haystack, fired four times when he ran, and the sheriff resisted threats of lynching.

accounts.label: Fisher's account
accounts.gist: He was chestnut hunting and playing with boys all Sunday, fled Monday after being warned Wolf was going to shoot him, and hid because he would have been killed had he given up.

accounts.label: Mrs. Wolf's account
accounts.gist: A man stepped from behind a tree on the woods path, fought her, threatened her with a knife, tied her and assaulted her; she identified Fisher at the hearing.

framing.detail: The Evening Star's Baltimore American special called Fisher 'the scoundrel' and said he had earned 'swift retribution'; the National Republican headed the first wire item 'A Candidate for Hemp.'
Der Deutsche Correspondent called him a 'black devil' and hoped he would not escape the citizens' thirst for revenge, criticizing the sheriff and the small reward.
Brief wire items ran as 'A Negro Ravisher Shot' and 'A Ravisher Shot', treating the accusation as fact.
The Somerset Herald printed Fisher's denial but added 'There is no doubt, however, that he is the scoundrel,' while praising the sheriff's resolve against a lynching.
